Catalytic Asymmetric Synthesis of Chiral Allenylic Fluorides Enabled
by Multiple Radical Sorting
Yingying Li, Xian Gong, Ye Yuan, Yuyang Bai, Huan Li, and Lingling Chu*
Abstract: Here, we disclose a nickel-catalyzed, three-
component asymmetric radical sorting strategy that
enables the enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral
allenylic fluorides from readily available 1,3-enynes, fluo-
roiodomethane, and alkyl bromides. This radical protocol
proceeds under mild, reductive conditions, accommo-
dates a broad range of functional groups, including those
found in complex bioactive molecules, and demonstrates
high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. A previously
unrecognized fluorine effect proved essential in dictating
both reactivity and stereocontrol in this multicomponent
radical coupling. This discovery establishes an efficient
protocol for enantioselective multiple radical sorting and
provides a modular platform for the catalytic synthesis of
fluorine-containing axial chirality.
The design of efficient synthetic methods to access struc-
turally diverse allenes continues to be a topic of great
significance in modern organic chemistry, owing to their
broad utility in pharmaceuticals and advanced materials.<sup>[1–3]</sup>

also serve as versatile synthetic intermediates amenable to

prevalence in natural products and their potential as chiral
ligands or bioactive compounds.<sup>[9–11]</sup> However, the selective
construction of such motifs—especially those bearing func-
tional handles for further elaboration—remains a formidable
synthetic challenge.<sup>[12–20]</sup> Within this context, axially chiral
fluorine-containing allenes,<sup>[21,22]</sup> such as allenylic fluorides,
represent an especially intriguing yet underexplored subclass.
Despite the rich chemistry of chiral allylic and propargylic
fluorides<sup>[23–26]</sup> and the rising importance of fluorinated motifs
in medicinal and materials chemistry,<sup>[27,28]</sup> general, and

are conspicuously lacking (Figure 1i). To date, only a racemic
example of allenylic fluorides has been reported via radi-
cal fluorination,<sup>[29]</sup> highlighting the pressing need for new
strategies to access these valuable scaffolds.

attention due to their ability to access reactivity modes com-

that can be readily generated through diverse pathways
and harnessed for C–C bond formation.<sup>[30–32]</sup> Among these

as particularly attractive, owing to the high reactivity of
the enyne motifs, their broad structural tunability, and
the accessibility of various radical precursors.<sup>[33]</sup> Despite
these advances, the asymmetric radical difunctionalization
of enynes remains largely underdeveloped (Figure 1ii).<sup>[19]</sup>
Existing examples have primarily relied on radical coupling

date, attempts involving alkyl halides have only afforded

pool of viable radical coupling partners—especially those
that enable both structural diversity and enantiocontrol—
is essential for broadening access to axially chiral allene
frameworks, including those bearing medicinally relevant
functional groups.

roiodomethane, and alkyl bromides. This radical protocol

dates a broad range of functional groups, including those
found in complex bioactive molecules, and demonstrates
high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. A previously
unrecognized fluorine effect proved essential in dictating
both reactivity and stereocontrol in this multicomponent
radical coupling. This discovery establishes an efficient
protocol for enantioselective multiple radical sorting and
provides a modular platform for the catalytic synthesis of
fluorine-containing axial chirality.

date, attempts involving alkyl halides have only afforded

pool of viable radical coupling partners—especially those

is essential for broadening access to axially chiral allene

functional groups.

valuable bioisostere for hydroxymethyl and methyl groups,
offering unique physicochemical properties with minimal
steric impact.<sup>[42]</sup> Despite their growing importance, effi-
cient catalytic strategies for the direct incorporation of
CH<sub>2</sub>F moieties into complex molecular scaffolds remain
underdeveloped.<sup>[43–46]</sup> This challenge stems largely from the

non-productive side reactions.<sup>[47–49]</sup> In contrast to the more
established protocols for asymmetric difluoromethylation and
trifluoromethylation,<sup>[50,51]</sup> enantioselective methods for CH<sub>2</sub>F
incorporation are still in their infancy.<sup>[52]</sup>
Inspired by our ongoing efforts in asymmetric radical
cross-couplings,<sup>[53–60]</sup> we envisioned a nickel-catalyzed asym-
metric multiple-radical sorting strategy<sup>[61–65]</sup> for enabling
an unprecedented enantioselective synthesis of axially chi-
ral allenylic fluorides from 1,3-enynes (Figure 1iii). We
hypothesized that fluoroiodomethane (ICH F), a stable and
readily available reagent, could serve as a source of CH F
radicals through halogen atom transfer (XAT) or single-
electron transfer (SET) pathways.<sup>[66–69]</sup> When paired with
a chiral nickel catalyst and a second carbon-based radical
precursor, this design could forge the target products in
a single operation through an orchestrated radical sorting
sequence. Implementing this design requires overcoming
several significant challenges. First, the concurrent genera-
tion and selective engagement of multiple carbon-centered
radicals—including CH<sub>2</sub>F, alkyl, propargyl, and allenyl rad-
ical species—demands stringent control to avoid competing
pathways such as hydrogen atom transfer, homocoupling, or
two-component cross-couplings.<sup>[70]</sup> Second, achieving stereo-
control in reactions involving highly reactive allenyl radicals
and fluoromethyl radicals remains particularly difficult, espe-
cially in the context of axial chirality.<sup>[71]</sup> Third, the risk of
forming unstable α-fluoro carbenoids from CH<sub>2</sub>F precursors
necessitates careful tuning of the reaction conditions to
prevent decomposition.<sup>[47–49]</sup> Herein, we report the successful

tive three-component radical dialkylation of enynes with
ICH F and alkyl bromides under mild reductive conditions

excellent chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Notably, a
distinct fluorine effect was uncovered, which proved critical
in governing both the reactivity and stereocontrol of this
multicomponent process.

With optimized conditions in hand, we next examined the
scope of this asymmetric radical sorting process. As outlined
in Scheme 1, a wide array of substituted 1,3-enynes partic-
ipated smoothly in the three-component coupling with two
different alkyl halides, alkyl bromide 2 and ICH F 3, affording
axially chiral allenylic fluorides with high levels of chemo-,
regio-, and enantioselectivity (4–21, up to 92% ee). The reac-
tion exhibited broad functional group tolerance under mild
conditions, accommodating ethers (4), esters (5–8), amides
(9), alkyl chlorides (11), silyl ethers (12), internal olefins (16),
thioethers (17), and lactams (19). A variety of heteroaromatic
motifs, including thiophenes (13), indoles (14), thiazoles (15),
and carbazoles (20), were also well-tolerated. Beyond alkyl-
substituted enynes, aryl-substituted analogs, including those
bearing electron-rich or deficient substituents, proved equally
effective and furnished the desired products in good yields
and high ee (22–28, up to 95% ee). Notably, aryl bromides
remained intact under the reaction conditions, offering a
valuable orthogonal handle for downstream derivatization
(25). Moreover, a ferrocenyl-substituted enyne delivered the
corresponding allenylic fluoride in 67% yield and 89% ee,
further demonstrating the method’s versatility (28).
To highlight the synthetic potential of this protocol,
particularly in the context of late-stage functionalization,
we explored a series of enyne derivatives derived from
bioactive molecules and pharmaceuticals under the standard
conditions. As shown in Scheme 1, substrates derived from
ciprofibrate (29), oxaprozin (30), pterostilbene (31), isoxepac
(32), febuxostat (33), indomethacin (34), and vitamin E (35)
all underwent efficient coupling with alkyl bromide 2 and
ICH F 3, affording the corresponding axially chiral allenylic
fluorides in high yields and excellent ee (up to 93% ee).
Finally, the scalability of this protocol was demonstrated
by performing the model reaction on a 3.0 mmol scale,
which furnished product 4 in a yield and enantiomeric
excess comparable to those of small-scale transformation
(Scheme 1).
We next sought to evaluate the generality of the alkyl
radical precursors (Scheme 2). As anticipated, a range
of tertiary α-halo carbonyl compounds, including both α-
bromo esters and α-bromo amides, proved to be competent
radical precursors, affording the desired axially chiral allene
products in good yields and with high ee (36–45, up to
92% ee). In addition to linear α-bromo carbonyl compounds,
sterically encumbered esters bearing cyclobutyl (38) or
cyclohexyl (39) substituents were also well-tolerated, deliv-
ering the corresponding chiral allenes efficiently. Moreover,
gem-difluoromethyl substituted alkyl halides, including 2-
bromo-2,2-difluoromethyl esters, amides, and phosphonates,
underwent the multicomponent coupling reaction with high
efficiency (40–45). The absolute configuration of product (S)-
45, ee of which is 99% after recrystallization, was unambigu-
ously confirmed by single-crystal X-ray crystallography,<sup>[72]</sup>
and the stereochemistry of the remaining products was
assigned by analogy. Encouragingly, secondary α-bromo
esters were also suitable coupling partners, delivering the
corresponding allenylic fluorides in moderate yield and high
ee (46, 78% yield, 91% ee, 82% ee). In these cases, the
diastereomeric ratio was approximately 1:1, consistent with
a radical mechanism involving non-stereospecific formation
of α-carbonyl radicals (46). Notably, even primary α-bromo
carbonyl compounds participated effectively in the trans-
formation, furnishing 1,4-dialkylated products with excellent
enantioselectivities, albeit with slightly reduced yields (47–
48). These results are particularly striking given the subtle
steric differences between the CH F radical and 1-alkyl
radicals, highlighting the chemoselectivity of this radical
sorting protocol.
